claims.statement: Categories and containers are both stored as adjacency lists — a nullable self-referencing `parent_id` with no depth, materialized path, or sibling-order column — and an item's location is a single `items.container_id` foreign key, so both the tree shape and the item's where-string are recomputed per request rather than stored.

`build_tree` in both repositories turns one flat, name-sorted row list into nested nodes: it sorts by name, partitions nodes into a children map or the roots list using an id-set guard that promotes orphans and NULL parents to roots, and attaches children recursively via `map.remove` so each node is consumed at most once.

`container::list_tree` and `category::list_tree` issue a single unbounded SELECT and assemble the nested DTO in Rust instead of using a recursive SQL query or per-level queries, so each `/containers/tree` and `/categories/tree` request loads the whole table and returns it name-sorted with no server-side cache.

Nodes that form a parent cycle (including a self-parent) are unreachable from any root during `build_tree`'s attach pass and are therefore silently omitted from the tree response while still present in the flat list endpoint, because neither the repositories, the handlers, nor the schema check ancestry when a `parent_id` is written.

`get_path` walks `parent_id` iteratively from the requested container up to the root, collecting one `PathSegment { id, name }` per step and then reversing the vector, so every caller receives a root→leaf path whose last element is the container itself.

`get_path` keeps no visited set, so a parent cycle or self-parent makes it loop indefinitely while growing the path vector; since item lists, item detail, and search hits resolve a path for every row, one such row hangs those requests instead of only breaking the affected container page.

Path resolution costs one SELECT per ancestor per call site and is neither cached nor deduplicated, so item list and search responses run `get_path` once per returned row, the container detail page requests up to 100 such rows, and `handlers::container::detail` fetches the container row twice (once via `get`, once as the first step of `get_path`).

The same `PathSegment` array produced by `get_path` is reused as the container breadcrumb (`ContainerDetail.path`), the item's '位置' row (`ItemDetail.container_path`), and the one-line location on item-list and search rows (`ItemSummary.container_path`), so all three surfaces agree by construction.

An item shows only its category's bare name (`category_name`, resolved by one scalar query) while it shows the container's full ancestor path, so the category hierarchy is navigation-only and never rendered as an item's classification path.

`flattenTree` depth-first flattens the server-provided tree into `{value,label,depth,path}` options whose `path` joins ancestor names with ' › ', and `Select` uses `depth` for 16px-per-level indentation, `path` as the trigger text of the chosen option, and `path + label` as the target of its searchable filter.

`flattenTree` feeds five pickers (category create, category edit, container edit, item create, item edit); every parent picker removes only the node being edited from its own options, so descendants stay selectable, and the top-level container create form offers no parent picker at all — child containers exist only via the detail page's form, which posts an explicit `parent_id`.

`containerPathText` joins path segments with ' › ' and returns '未归位' for an empty or missing path, which is how items with `container_id = NULL` are labelled on item cards and search hits, while the container breadcrumb and item '位置' row instead link each segment individually and print plain 未归位.

Deleting a container or category nullifies references before deleting the row — items lose their container/category and children keep existing with `parent_id` set to NULL — so deletion promotes children to roots rather than deleting them, reparenting them to the grandparent, or touching items inside those subtrees.

`container::delete` never unlinks the file referenced by `containers.image_path`, unlike `item::delete` which unlinks each image and thumbnail, so deleting a container leaves its photo orphaned on disk.

Only item create/update/delete and the startup `sync_all` write `items_fts`, so renaming or deleting a container or category leaves the indexed `container_name`, `container_label`, and `category_name` stale until the process restarts.

`container_type` is a free-form TEXT column defaulting to 'other' with no CHECK constraint or server validation (create substitutes 'other' only when the field is absent), while the SPA hard-codes eight options — room, table, shelf, box, drawer, cabinet, bag, other — inline in three components and renders the stored identifier raw instead of its Chinese label.

Container-type defaults differ by entry point: the `/containers` create form initialises to 'room' while the child-container form initialises to 'box', so the DB default 'other' is only reachable through direct API use.

`container::update` merges with `.or(existing)` / `.unwrap_or(&existing)`, so an omitted or null `parent_id`, `label`, or `description` keeps the stored value; combined with the edit form sending `parentId || undefined`, a container can be reparented but can never be promoted back to a top-level root through `PUT /containers/{id}` or the edit form.

`GET /containers/{id}` returns the container, its path, one level of children, and only the first 100 items stored directly in that container (page 1, size 100, total discarded), and item-list/search container filtering is exact-match on `container_id`, so no endpoint aggregates items across a subtree.

`build_tree` is duplicated in the category and container repositories instead of being shared, and the category copy still declares a `remaining` vector that is never populated before being appended to the roots, so any change to tree semantics must be mirrored in both files.

Tree behaviour has no automated coverage: `server/tests` is empty, `cargo test -p server` compiles no tests, and tree assembly, path derivation, and delete outcomes are verified manually through the API and UI.
